title: Where to Start with Economic History
dek: Seven books, ordered from first step to deep end.

slides.heading: Start Short
slides.body: Robert C. Allen's *Global Economic History: A Very Short Introduction* covers why some countries got rich and others did not, in under 200 pages. The best single map of the field.

slides.heading: Europe Before the Machines
slides.body: Carlo Cipolla reconstructs the European economy between 1000 and 1700: population, prices, guilds, plague. It shows how a pre-industrial economy actually worked, before growth became normal.

slides.heading: One City, Read Closely
slides.body: Frederic Lane's *Venice: A Maritime Republic* follows a merchant state through its galleys, banks and state-run convoys. Economic history at the scale of a single, extraordinarily well-documented city.

slides.heading: The Long Duration
slides.body: Braudel's *Civilization and Capitalism* moves from daily bread to world trade in three volumes. Its central claim: markets and capitalism are different things, and capitalism lives at the top.

slides.heading: Why Rules Matter
slides.body: Douglass North argues that institutions, the formal and informal rules of a society, explain long-run economic performance better than resources or technology alone. A Nobel framework in a short book.

slides.heading: Why Europe, Why Then
slides.body: Kenneth Pomeranz argues that the Yangzi delta and England looked similar until about 1800, and that coal and colonies made the difference. Later wage and output data have challenged the timing.

slides.heading: Ideas as Causes
slides.body: Joel Mokyr's *A Culture of Growth* locates the origins of modern growth in an intellectual market: the Republic of Letters, where useful knowledge competed and accumulated across borders.

cta_line: Every week the Substack takes one of these debates further, with the sources laid out so you can check them.
caption:
Economic history is the part of the past that left the most data behind.

Start with Allen for the map, Cipolla for the pre-industrial baseline, then Braudel (1979) and North (1990) for the two big frameworks. Pomeranz (2000) is the debate everyone still argues with.

Comment READ and I will send you the Substack link.
